b: On November 7th, ICE agents in Los Angeles took a man in their custody to Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Boyle Heights, a neighborhood which is more than 90 percent Hispanic and Latino.

ICE, the hospital, and local activists dispute much of what happened that day. On social media, some activists alleged that ICE, when not given free rein of the hospital, purposefully retaliated against the community. Regardless of which combination of actions happened and with what intent, three things occurred which no one really disputes.
First, ICE agents blocked access to the Adventist Health White’s Emergency Room for approximately two hours. According to the hospital:

Federal agents brought a person in their custody to our emergency department, and we cared for that patient with dignity and privacy, as we do for every patient. When agents formed a line across our ambulance entrance, which we did not request nor authorize, we diverted ambulances to nearby hospitals for about two hours to ensure every patient received timely care.

“White Memorial,” the hospital spokesperson insisted, “does not participate in immigration enforcement. We know last night frightened our neighbors. No matter what happens outside our doors, everyone who comes inside is our patient, and our focus will only be on that patient, and it will not change.”

Second, around the same time, local residents got word that ICE was at the hospital. As has happened across Southern California, Minneapolis, and around the nation in recent years, rapid response community defense measures kicked in. As Boyle Heights Beat reported, activists on the scene included Abraham Zavala of the group Union del Barrio. Zavala, who was born at Adventist Health White (as were his children), described it as “sacred ground.” At least two protesters, both of whom are U.S. citizens, were then detained by ICE, according to the Boyle Heights Immigration Rights Network.

And third, the intended damage was done: ICE wanted people to be frightened and they are, understandably, frightened. We will never know if any (or how many) people died during those two hours when the ER was not available at Adventist Health White. We will never know if someone’s life will be shortened by months or years because they couldn’t access emergency care that Saturday night. And we certainly won’t ever know who didn’t seek care at all that night because they saw on TikTok or on the local news that ICE had blocked access to their neighborhood hospital.
It may make Latinos think twice about getting medical care, or possibly forgo it entirely—especially if their immigration status makes them vulnerable.

ICE blocking that ER is a very tangible example of how medical racism manifests: armed agents of the state not only threatened to arrest anyone seeking care in the hospital, but they physically blocked access to all medical care in a Latino neighborhood. Such nasty work is rarely done so brazenly, and ICE’s harm that night is just a beginning.

How that harm will manifest is unpredictable. It may make Latinos think twice about getting medical care, or possibly forgo it entirely—especially if their immigration status makes them vulnerable. It may make undocumented family members less likely to accompany their ill relatives to the hospital, resulting in potentially substandard care. If racism is, as Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes, “the state-sanctioned or extralegal production and exploitation of group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death,” the seed planted that one night will likely result in medical health disparities and in needlessly premature deaths.

Narratives entwining health and racism are powerful. I grew up not too far from Boyle Heights, in the city of Oxnard, another majority-Mexican American community. The threat of raids and the occupation of a hospital ER will, no doubt, make worse an ongoing problem. Too many children in my hometown are not going to school because their parents fear some member of their family will be abducted en route. When I talk to Latinx medical providers—from a dentist in Oxnard to an eye doctor in Queens, New York—they tell me how empty their once-full calendars have become. Many of their Latinx patients are simply forgoing teeth cleanings or eye exams (or pap smears or mammograms) because the narrative is working: ICE can grab you anywhere, so you better stay put as much as possible. (Similarly, a recently deported gay immigrant told me that when he was cooped up for months avoiding ICE, he stopped taking the HIV-prevention medication PrEP, and then became HIV-positive.) In just one night, ICE amplified the narrative that seeking medical care can cost you the ultimate health penalty: arrest, possible deportation, and separation from your loved ones.

This is not a new situation in America, and it reminds me of a narrative born from the too-short life and tragic death of Dr. Charles Drew. Despite only living about 46 years. Dr. Drew was one of the most accomplished African American physicians in history. The narrative of his death also bloomed in predictable ways.
Like many Black children of my age, I learned about the mythology of Dr. Drew as a child, and was wowed and chilled by the irony of his death.

Prior to enrolling in medical school at McGill in the late 1920s, young Drew had already worked teaching biology and chemistry at the university level. Upon completing his MD, he joined the faculty of Howard Medical School and became a surgeon at Freedman’s Hospital in D.C., where he dedicated himself to the health of Black people. He then pursued a Doctor of Science at Columbia, where he wrote his dissertation, Banked Blood: A Study on Blood Preservation. While blood banks existed, they were not very effective. Medical science and the lay public had long imagined different races of people to have different types of blood. Even though the four major blood types (A,B, AB and O) had been discovered at the turn of the 20th century, many scientists and scientific organizations nonsensically segregated blood by race. Primitive blood banks had been used in World War I, but not knowing what blood type the wounded possessed (“dog tags” didn’t start listing blood type until the 1940s), combined with the crude storage techniques, made shock and infection common, which rendered transfusions of limited use.
Yet, despite his enormous achievements, racism haunted Drew throughout his career and—through the power of narrative—long after his death.

In the 1930s, Dr. Drew made a major breakthrough which broadly benefited all of humanity: he discovered how to separate blood plasma from the red and white cells of blood, and how to store it safely in such a way that it could be used for up to two months. Because anyone could be given plasma in an emergency, regardless of their blood type, his findings exponentially increased the life-saving capacity of blood transfusions. He also invented the “bloodmobile,” expanding how donations could be collected. Thus, Dr. Drew became the “father of the modern blood bank,” and the Allied Powers used his techniques to save countless lives in WWII.
Yet, despite his enormous achievements, racism haunted Drew throughout his career and—through the power of narrative—long after his death.

Drew was appointed the first director of the American Red Cross’s blood bank program in 1941. However, when the powers that be insisted that blood from “Negro donors” be rejected unless it was stored separately, he resigned in 1942.

Every year for more than a decade, Dr. Drew would travel to a free clinic in Tuskegee, Alabama, providing free surgery for poor Black people. In 1950, he and three other Black doctors drove more than 700 miles from D.C. to perform this service. On the last night of the clinic, he worked overnight in the operating theater. Then, he got into his car, drove home, and fell asleep at the wheel. After flipping several times, the car crashed in a field.
The other three doctors in the car with him that night suffered minor injuries, but Dr. Drew was in a bad way. And here, many Black children my age likely heard some version of the following myth:
Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, and was denied a blood transfusion…even though he had invented the process for using plasma in this way.
Or, Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, and they had his blood type…but the hospital wouldn’t give it to him, because it was “white blood” and they didn’t have any “Negro blood.”
Or, Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, which was segregated…and they were out of “Negro beds,” and while being transported to a Negro hospital, he died in the ambulance.

In truth, according to the three other doctors who were with him that night, Dr. Drew received immediate and competent care at the nearest hospital. Dr. John Ford, his friend who survived the crash, said Drew’s injuries were so severe that nothing could have saved him.

But the myths were born because they revealed much that was true (in the manner that “myths” are not false stories, but stories which reveal broad truths about history and society). Dr. Drew had been pushed out of the American Red Cross because of the segregation of “Negro blood” (a policy the organization continued until after his death). Black people routinely did die in the Jim Crow south because there weren’t “Negro beds” available, because the best resourced hospitals were segregated, and because of longer ambulance ride times. And Dr. Drew himself was a victim of the “state-sanctioned or extralegal production and exploitation of group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death” at least in part because of racism. Consider that he traveled to Tuskegee (a city synonymous with another horrific instance of medical racism) because there was not sufficient healthcare there for Black Americans, that he had to work all night because of this paucity of care, and that he was forced to drive home exhausted because there were few or no motels for Black people on his segregated driving route.

Narratives play a huge role in revealing fundamental truths, regardless of the exact incident which may incite them. Whether or not individual ICE agents meant to intimidate Latinos on November 7th is irrelevant; care was suppressed and people were made to feel intimidated in ways that will resonate in lethal ways for years to come. Similarly, how exactly Dr. Drew died did not stop African Americans, hearing of the death of the most prominent Black doctor of his time, from understanding that racism played a role in it. When racism and access to medical care collide, it is not only the actual subpar care that kills people, it is also the narratives that then affect people’s behavior. This manifests as the person who doesn’t call 911 because they’re worried the first responder might arrest their undocumented mother. Or the Black person afraid they have a sexually-transmitted infection who doesn’t trust going to a clinic. Or a would-be patient too frightened to approach a hospital because they have good reason to believe they may be made to feel unwelcome (or turned away entirely) if they are transgender, immigrant, or Black.

Narratives are powerful. One I have been suspicious of is the story that the Democratic Party is the anti-ICE party. Many mid-term voters cast their ballots for Democrats seemingly under the belief that ICE was the creation of Republicans while Democrats are the anti-ICE party. (Seeing people place “I Voted” stickers on the death sites of Rene Goode and Alex Pretti seemed especially egregious considering that for decades, Democrats have repeatedly funded the kinds of immigration agents who killed them.)
Then, on election night, I saw the Democratic U.S. Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan promise to “rip ICE apart.”
Godspeed to her and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. Maybe as Senators they can help write a new narrative—one where racism and access to medical care are no longer intertwined, but ripped apart.
